Gabriela Hearst often turns her collection development into an anthropology project. For the spring season, she embarked on a study of 100 years of Afghan women, from the late Emirate period, through eras of reform and war, up to the current moment of Taliban control after a couple of decades of US intervention. Under Taliban rule, women’s circumstances in the country have deteriorated; Hearst quoted a statistic that the female literacy rate is just 37%. She wanted to bring international attention to the situation, as well as to the country’s rich textile- and jewelry-making traditions.

Her collaborators in the endeavor include Shoshana Stewart of Turquoise Mountain, a nonprofit organization that connects the country’s artisans to international designers, and Fara Homidi, the Afghanistan-born, California-bred makeup artist and beauty brand owner.

Hearst called the hand-painted miniatures encased in crystal and silver and used as buttons on her signature tailoring “the heart of the collection.” Their delicate beauty is hard to detect in these pictures, but they reward a zoom-in; the little works of art elevated everything they embellished. Among the other decorative motifs inspired by Afghan tradition here were the shisha mirrors (used to ward off the evil eye), which decorated the white pantsuit that opened the show (St. Vincent performed in its black counterpart) and the crochet and knit dresses that followed it. The colorful dresses at the end, meanwhile, reproduced the motifs found in Suzani and Hazara textiles via paintings by Sughra Hussainy, a US-based Afghan artist.

All of this was handled respectfully. Still, there’s an optics risk involved for a designer incorporating another culture’s traditions into her own work. What Hearst has going in her favor is a long practice of collaborating with artisans around the world, including Manos del Uruguay, in her home country. Also, she said her involvement with Turquoise Mountain will be ongoing.

Beyond the Afghan influences, other elements here reflected nice forward progress. The hems of knit dresses extended up to encircle the shoulders like a shawl: complicated patternmaking with effortlessly elegant results. Long suede slips in chartreuse and jade as well as stripy knit dresses had a similarly unstudied appeal. Also charming: the little leather pouches strung on necklaces and the safety pin brooches worn at shirt collars that were embellished with semiprecious quartz, lapis lazuli, and malachite beads made by Turquoise Mountain artisans.
